summary: Nasavior is an interactive atlas of NASA microgravity combustion experiments for engineers planning spacecraft, stations, Moon and Mars habitats and pressurized rovers. It summarizes, ranks and interprets 26 experiments (24 NASA PSI investigations plus 2 NTRS entries) and 55 page-cited measurements. The user picks an environment and sets oxygen, pressure and air flow. Nasavior then shows the experiments that match, compares the chosen oxygen level with limits NASA measured at the same gravity, contrasts 0 g with 1 g, and shows where NASA has no data. In BASS-II on the ISS, PMMA kept burning at 13.6 percent oxygen against a 1 g limit of 16 percent. For the Moon and Mars, every 0.16 g and 0.38 g limit comes from 5-second drop-tower tests, so Nasavior shows that gap instead of filling it. Every value is transcribed from a NASA document and shown with its source and page. Nothing is extrapolated and no text is generated, so missing data is reported as a research gap. This matters because a fire test on Earth is not always conservative for space.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Nasavior is a web dashboard built on NASA microgravity combustion data. The user chooses a target environment (ISS, Lunar base, Martian habitat, pressurized rover or Earth baseline) and sets oxygen, pressure and air flow. Nasavior then does three things the challenge asks for. It summarizes: a cited summary for the chosen environment and an Atlas of 26 experiments (24 NASA PSI investigations and 2 NTRS entries) with objectives, hardware and findings. It ranks: experiments are ordered by how closely their recorded gravity, oxygen, pressure and flow match the user's selection, with the reasons shown. It interprets: the chosen oxygen level is compared with limits NASA measured at the same gravity, 0 g is compared with 1 g sample by sample, and the Moon and Mars data gap is mapped. A search box, Ask the Atlas, retrieves records and answers only with text copied from them.

WHAT THE DATA SHOWS

BASS-II on the ISS: a PMMA rod kept burning at 13.6 percent oxygen in microgravity, while the 1 g blowoff limit is 16 percent. Saffire-II: no silicone sample (0.27 to 1.03 mm) spread in microgravity at about 22 percent oxygen and 20 cm/s, although the thinnest burned completely in 1 g, so reduced gravity is not uniformly worse. Drop-tower tests at Martian and Lunar gravity gave negative oxygen margins versus 1 g for Mylar, Ultem and Nomex. All 0.16 g and 0.38 g records are 5-second drop tests, and none lies inside the lunar atmosphere envelope (oxygen at or above 30 percent, pressure at or below 10.2 psi). NASA plans the first combustion experiments on the Moon (FM2) for late 2026.

WHY IT IS DIFFERENT

Engineers need to know what NASA has tested and what it has not. Every number is transcribed by hand from a NASA document and shown with its reference and page. A limit is shown only for the gravity level where it was measured, never extrapolated. Mars habitat and rover atmospheres are flagged as assumptions because the sources do not define them. The app reports missing data as a result, for example when asked about a material the dataset never mentions. Known limitations are listed in the app and in the repository.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

A fast, auditable way to find relevant NASA fire-safety evidence for crewed vehicles and habitats, and a clear list of what still has to be measured, especially in partial gravity. PSI also reports Earth benefits (cleaner, more efficient combustion; fire detection and suppression models), which the app shows.

TOOLS

Python 3.13, Streamlit, Plotly, pandas, NumPy, pydantic, PyYAML and rank-bm25 (keyword retrieval). No machine learning model and no external API run inside the app, so it needs no API key. Data work: NASA PSI public API and NASA NTRS papers read by hand. Fonts: Inter and JetBrains Mono. Tests: pytest (98 tests).

TEAM AND PROCESS

Muhammed Esat Demir: software and product (application, interface, deployment). Kevser Demir: data and science (NASA source review, data extraction and verification).
